lesson.menu_title: How Sure Are You? — Forecasts, Polls and the Language of Doubt
lesson.menu_desc: A three-point lead, a two-point margin, and the words that tell your listener how much to trust you -- 33 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 9 -- How Sure Are You?
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Henrique Monteiro Neto | Lesson 9 -- How Sure Are You?

listenings.text: Let me take the two things people find hardest, slowly. The first is the sample. A properly randomised sample of about a thousand people gives you a margin of roughly three points, and that is true whether the country has ten million voters or two hundred million. People do not believe this and it is nonetheless the case. The second thing is what that margin covers. It covers sampling, and only sampling. It says nothing at all about how the question was worded, nothing about who refused to answer, and nothing about who will actually turn out on the day. Those three are, in my experience, where the real errors live. So my rule of thumb, a week before a vote, is simple. Take the published margin and double it. If the answer still gives you a clear winner, you may say so.

Here is the thing that should worry you, and it is the opposite of what most people expect. If every poll in the final week agrees to within half a point, do not read that as certainty. Read it as herding. What happens is not fraud and it is not usually even conscious. It is that being wrong on your own costs a pollster their reputation, and being wrong together with everybody else costs nothing at all. So the incentives push quietly towards the middle. And the poll that sits three points away from the pack, the outlier that everybody laughs at on the evening news, is quite often the only one that has not adjusted itself. It is also the one that nobody wants to publish.

extra_audio.text: Rachel says the sentence she most dislikes is that the polls were wrong. He observes that saying so sounds like an excuse prepared in advance. She agrees that it is prepared in advance, and says that is the whole point of a margin of error. He points out that the headline still says three points ahead. She says she would ban the decimal point, because false precision does more damage than a wrong forecast.
